subject: science
verification_note: cde.ca.gov blocks automated fetches (web-firewall redirect), so these topics were written from knowledge of the California standards and NOT checked against the page; the listed sources are where to verify them. Review in a browser before relying on it.
note: California NGSS-style science topics, K-5 by grade and 6-8 by an integrated-model grade placement (6: ecosystems, energy, climate, plate tectonics; 7: cells, atoms, reactions, resources; 8: forces, waves, genetics, evolution, space), written from general knowledge of CA NGSS; the CDE pages could not be fetched at authoring time, so placement of grades 6-8 should be verified.

items.subject: science
items.title: Pushes and pulls
items.summary: A push moves something away and a pull brings it closer. Try pushing a toy car, then pulling it. A bigger push makes it go faster!

items.subject: science
items.title: Motion words
items.summary: Let's learn words about moving things! Things can push, pull, roll, slide, and spin.

items.subject: science
items.title: The Sun warms the Earth
items.summary: The Sun sends light that warms the ground, the water, and you. That's why a sidewalk gets hot in the sun but a shady spot stays cool.

items.subject: science
items.title: What plants need
items.summary: Plants need water, light, and air to grow. Without them a plant gets droopy and sad. Do you water a plant at home?

items.subject: science
items.title: What animals need
items.summary: Animals need food, water, air, and a safe place to live. People are animals too, and we need the same things!

items.subject: science
items.title: Watching the weather
items.summary: Weather is what the air outside is doing today: sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, or snowy. Look out the window. What's the weather right now?

items.subject: science
items.title: Weather words
items.summary: Here are weather words! Weather can be sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, or stormy.

items.subject: science
items.title: Living and nonliving
items.summary: Living things grow, need food, and change. A cat and a tree are living. A rock and a ball are not. Can you spot something living near you?

items.subject: science
items.title: Animals change their home
items.summary: Animals change the land around them. Beavers build dams, and birds build nests. People change the land too, when we build houses and roads.

items.subject: science
items.title: Taking care of water
items.summary: Water is precious, especially in California where it can get very dry. We can turn off the tap while brushing teeth to save water.

items.subject: science
items.title: Weather and safety
items.summary: Some weather can be dangerous, like strong wind or a big storm. Grown-ups listen to weather reports so everyone can stay safe.

items.subject: science
items.title: Tide pool animals
items.summary: At California beaches, tide pools are little puddles left when the ocean goes out. Sea stars, crabs, and anemones live in them. Look gently and never pull them off!

items.subject: science
items.title: Fix a problem
items.summary: Engineers solve problems by making things. If rain wets your friend, you could design an umbrella or a shelter. What problem would you fix?

items.subject: science
items.title: Tall trees
items.summary: California's coast redwoods are the tallest trees on Earth, some are over 350 feet, taller than a 30-story building!

items.subject: science
items.title: Sound is a shake
items.summary: Sound comes from things that vibrate, which means shake back and forth very fast. Touch your throat while you hum and you can feel it!

items.subject: science
items.title: Sound words
items.summary: Let's learn sound words! Sounds can be loud or quiet, high or low.

items.subject: science
items.title: Light helps us see
items.summary: We see things because light bounces off them into our eyes. With no light at all, like in a closed closet, we can't see anything.

items.subject: science
items.title: See-through and blocking
items.summary: Some things let light pass through, like clear glass. Some block it and make a shadow, like a book. Some let a little through, like wax paper.

items.subject: science
items.title: Plant parts
items.summary: Plants have parts that do jobs! Roots drink water, stems hold the plant up, and leaves catch sunlight.

items.subject: science
items.title: Animal body parts for survival
items.summary: Animals have parts that help them live. Birds have wings to fly, fish have fins to swim, and rabbits have big ears to hear danger.

items.subject: science
items.title: Parents and babies
items.summary: Baby plants and animals look a lot like their parents but are not exactly the same. Puppies look like dogs, and a baby sunflower grows into a tall sunflower.

items.subject: science
items.title: Sun, moon, and stars patterns
items.summary: The Sun rises in the morning and sets in the evening. The Moon and stars come out at night. These patterns repeat every day.

items.subject: science
items.title: Longer and shorter days
items.summary: In summer the Sun stays up longer, so days are long. In winter the days are shorter. This pattern happens every year.

items.subject: science
items.title: The changing Moon
items.summary: The Moon looks different through the month, from a thin curve to a big circle. It's the same Moon, we just see a different amount of its sunny side.

items.subject: science
items.title: Tide pool survival
items.summary: Mussels on California rocks hold on with strong threads so waves can't wash them away. Body parts that help animals survive are called adaptations.

items.subject: science
items.title: Make a sound signal
items.summary: Engineers can make a tool to send a message far away. A drum, a whistle, or a flashlight can send signals when we can't shout.

items.subject: science
items.title: Hummingbirds in California
items.summary: Anna's hummingbird lives in California all year. Its long thin beak reaches deep into flowers to sip sweet nectar.

items.subject: science
items.title: Sun safety
items.summary: The Sun is a star, the closest one to us. Never look right at it. Sunglasses and hats help keep your eyes and skin safe.

items.subject: science
items.title: Solid, liquid, gas
items.summary: Matter comes as solid, liquid, or gas. Ice is solid, water is liquid, and steam is gas. Heating or cooling can change one into another!

items.subject: science
items.title: Material words
items.summary: Let's describe stuff! Materials can be hard or soft, rough or smooth, flexible or stiff.

items.subject: science
items.title: Melting and freezing
items.summary: Heat melts ice into water, and cooling freezes water back into ice. Even melted chocolate can harden again when cool. Some changes can be undone!

items.subject: science
items.title: Little pieces build big things
items.summary: Small pieces can be put together to make something new, like bricks making a wall. We can take them apart and build something different.

items.subject: science
items.title: How seeds travel
items.summary: Plants can't walk, so seeds hitch a ride. Wind blows dandelion fluff, animals carry burrs on fur, and squirrels bury acorns that grow into oaks.

items.subject: science
items.title: Pollinators
items.summary: Bees and other animals visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen from flower to flower. That helps plants make seeds and fruit.

items.subject: science
items.title: Habitats
items.summary: A habitat is a place where plants and animals live and find what they need. Deserts, forests, and oceans are all different habitats with different living things.

items.subject: science
items.title: California habitats
items.summary: California has many habitats close together: foggy redwood forests, hot deserts, snowy mountains, and rocky coast tide pools.

items.subject: science
items.title: Land and water
items.summary: Earth has land and water. We can show them on a map. Landforms include mountains, hills, valleys, and islands. Bodies of water include oceans, lakes, and rivers.

items.subject: science
items.title: Landform words
items.summary: Here are landform words! A hill is smaller than a mountain, and a valley is low land between them.

items.subject: science
items.title: Slow and fast changes
items.summary: Earth changes all the time. Volcanoes and floods change land fast. Wind and water wearing down rock changes it very slowly, over thousands of years.

items.subject: science
items.title: Earthquakes in California
items.summary: California has earthquakes because pieces of Earth's crust slide past each other. If one happens, remember: drop, cover, and hold on.

items.subject: science
items.title: Water in different places
items.summary: Water is found as liquid in oceans and rivers, and as solid ice on tall mountains like California's Sierra Nevada. Snow there melts in spring and fills rivers.

items.subject: science
items.title: Test and compare
items.summary: Engineers build, test, and then make it better. If you build two paper bridges, see which holds more toy cars. Testing shows which design works best.

items.subject: science
items.title: Dry spells in California
items.summary: Sometimes California gets very little rain for years, which is called drought. People then save water and plants and animals have to cope.

items.subject: science
items.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
items.summary: When pushes and pulls are equal and opposite, a thing stays still. When one is stronger, the thing moves. Tug-of-war shows this: the stronger side wins.

items.subject: science
items.title: Patterns in motion
items.summary: A swing moves back and forth in a regular pattern. If we watch the pattern, we can predict where it will be next.

items.subject: science
items.title: Magnets
items.summary: Magnets pull on some metals like iron, and they can push or pull other magnets without touching. Two north ends push apart, while north and south pull together.

items.subject: science
items.title: Force words
items.summary: Let's learn force words! Friction is a rubbing force that slows things down, and gravity pulls everything toward Earth.

items.subject: science
items.title: Life cycles
items.summary: Living things grow and change through life cycles. A butterfly goes from egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly. Different animals have different cycles.

items.subject: science
items.title: Traits and inheritance
items.summary: Traits are features like fur color or leaf shape. Young plants and animals get traits from their parents, but each one is a little bit different.

items.subject: science
items.title: Differences help survive
items.summary: In a group of the same kind of animal, each one is a little different. Sometimes those differences, like color, help one hide better or find more food.

items.subject: science
items.title: Adaptations to habitats
items.summary: Living things have features that fit their home. A desert kangaroo rat survives with very little water, and a polar bear's thick fur keeps it warm.

items.subject: science
items.title: Fossils
items.summary: Fossils are the remains or prints of living things from long ago, kept in rock. They show us what lived on Earth before people.

items.subject: science
items.title: La Brea Tar Pits
items.summary: In Los Angeles, tar bubbling up from the ground trapped animals thousands of years ago. Scientists have found saber-toothed cats, mammoths, and dire wolves there.

items.subject: science
items.title: Weather and climate
items.summary: Weather is what happens today. Climate is the usual weather in a place over many years. Los Angeles has a warm dry climate, while Alaska has a cold one.

items.subject: science
items.title: Weather hazards
items.summary: Some weather can cause harm, like floods, heavy storms, or wildfires in dry hot weather. Engineers design ways to lower the harm, like firebreaks and levees.

items.subject: science
items.title: Wildfires in California
items.summary: In California's long dry summers, plants dry out and fires can spread fast. Firefighters, and careful campers, help keep everyone safe. Some plants even need fire to sprout seeds.

items.subject: science
items.title: Designing a solution
items.summary: Engineers list what a solution must do, then try different ideas and compare. A good design meets the goal even when it has limits like cost and time.

items.subject: science
items.title: California condors
items.summary: The California condor is a huge bird that nearly went extinct in the 1980s. Scientists and zoos helped raise chicks, and now condors fly free again in California.

items.subject: science
items.title: Energy and speed
items.summary: Moving things have energy. The faster something moves, the more energy it has. A speeding bike is harder to stop than a slow one.

items.subject: science
items.title: Energy moves around
items.summary: Energy can pass from place to place by sound, light, heat, or electric current. Rubbing your hands makes them warm because motion energy turns into heat.

items.subject: science
items.title: Collisions
items.summary: When two things bump, energy passes from one to the other. A moving marble hitting a still marble makes it roll, and the first slows down.

items.subject: science
items.title: Energy words
items.summary: Let's learn energy words! Energy comes from sources like the Sun, wind, and fuel.

items.subject: science
items.title: Waves
items.summary: Waves carry energy without carrying water along. A ball floating on the ocean mostly bobs up and down as the wave passes beneath it.

items.subject: science
items.title: Sending information
items.summary: People send information using patterns, like Morse code, or by turning light and sound into signals. Fiber optic cables send messages as flashes of light.

items.subject: science
items.title: Structures that help animals
items.summary: Animals have body parts for surviving: eyes, ears, and noses gather information, and the brain decides what to do. Plants have thorns and roots that protect and feed them.

items.subject: science
items.title: Sense and survive words
items.summary: Let's learn words about how living things sense the world! Animals sense by seeing, hearing, smelling, and feeling.

items.subject: science
items.title: Weathering and erosion
items.summary: Wind, water, and ice break rock into smaller pieces, and moving water carries them away. Over millions of years this carved the Grand Canyon.

items.subject: science
items.title: Yosemite's glaciers
items.summary: Huge slow rivers of ice called glaciers carved Yosemite Valley long ago. They left steep granite walls like El Capitan and Half Dome.

items.subject: science
items.title: Fossils and rock layers
items.summary: Rock layers form over time, with older layers usually on the bottom. Fossils in the layers show that places once looked different, like seas where land is now.

items.subject: science
items.title: Earthquakes and volcanoes
items.summary: Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near the edges of Earth's giant crust pieces. California sits near one such edge, where the San Andreas Fault runs.

items.subject: science
items.title: San Andreas Fault
items.summary: The San Andreas Fault is a long crack in California where two crust pieces slowly slide past each other. When they suddenly slip, we feel an earthquake. Scientists use maps to prepare.

items.subject: science
items.title: Sources of energy
items.summary: We get energy from sources like sunlight, wind, water, coal, and oil. Some are renewable and won't run out, like sun and wind. California has many solar farms and wind turbines.

items.subject: science
items.title: Earthquake-safe buildings
items.summary: Engineers design buildings to sway, not snap, in earthquakes. They test models on shake tables and keep improving them.

items.subject: science
items.title: Matter is made of tiny particles
items.summary: All matter is made of tiny particles too small to see. Air looks empty but is full of them. A balloon grows when more air particles are inside.

items.subject: science
items.title: Mass doesn't disappear
items.summary: When ice melts, or sugar dissolves in water, the total amount of matter stays the same. Weigh before and after and it's equal.

items.subject: science
items.title: Properties of materials
items.summary: Materials have properties like color, hardness, how well they conduct heat or electricity, and whether they dissolve. Scientists use properties to tell materials apart.

items.subject: science
items.title: Mixing and reacting
items.summary: Mixing can just combine things, like salt in water. But sometimes a new substance forms, like when baking soda and vinegar fizz. That's a chemical reaction.

items.subject: science
items.title: Matter words
items.summary: Let's learn words about matter! A mixture is two or more things together, and a solution is a mixture where one thing dissolves.

items.subject: science
items.title: Energy from food
items.summary: Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and air. Animals eat plants or other animals to get energy. So the Sun's energy ends up in your lunch!

items.subject: science
items.title: Food chains and webs
items.summary: A food chain shows who eats what: grass, rabbit, then fox. Many chains connect into a food web. Decomposers like fungi break down dead things and return nutrients to soil.

items.subject: science
items.title: Ecosystem words
items.summary: Let's learn ecosystem words! An ecosystem is all the living and nonliving things in a place working together.

items.subject: science
items.title: Kelp forest ecosystem
items.summary: Off California's coast, giant kelp grows tall underwater, feeding and sheltering fish, otters, and urchins. Sea otters eat urchins, which keeps the kelp from being overgrazed.

items.subject: science
items.title: Gravity
items.summary: Gravity pulls things toward the center of Earth, which is why things fall down no matter where you are on the planet. Earth's gravity keeps the Moon circling us.

items.subject: science
items.title: The Sun is a star
items.summary: The Sun looks bigger and brighter than other stars only because it's so close. Other stars are very far away, and some are much bigger than the Sun.

items.subject: science
items.title: Day, night, and seasons
items.summary: Earth spinning makes day and night, and its tilt as it circles the Sun makes seasons. Shadows change length through the day because the Sun's height changes.

items.subject: science
items.title: Earth's four systems
items.summary: Earth has the geosphere (rock), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), and biosphere (life). They interact, like rain wearing rock and plants growing in soil.

items.subject: science
items.title: Where the water is
items.summary: Most of Earth's water is salty ocean. Only a tiny bit is fresh and usable. California gets much of its fresh water from snowpack melting in the Sierra Nevada.

items.subject: science
items.title: Protecting Earth's resources
items.summary: People can protect land, water, air, and living things by recycling, saving water, and cleaning up. Communities can design solutions and test which one helps most.

items.subject: science
items.title: Matter and energy in ecosystems
items.summary: Energy from the Sun flows through ecosystems as organisms eat each other, while matter like carbon and nitrogen is recycled again and again.

items.subject: science
items.title: Populations and resources
items.summary: Populations of living things grow or shrink depending on food, water, and space. When resources run short, competition increases, and the population can drop.

items.subject: science
items.title: Heat and temperature
items.summary: Heat is energy moving from warmer to cooler things. Temperature measures how fast particles are moving on average. Metal spoons feel cold because they pull heat away from your hand quickly.

items.subject: science
items.title: Weather, climate, and oceans
items.summary: The Sun heats Earth unevenly, so air and water currents move heat around. This drives weather and climate. Oceans store a lot of heat and shape coastal weather.

items.subject: science
items.title: California's climate
items.summary: California has a Mediterranean climate with wet winters and dry summers. Cold ocean currents and coastal fog keep the coast cool while inland valleys get hot.

items.subject: science
items.title: Plate tectonics
items.summary: Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that move slowly, only a few centimeters a year. Where they meet we get earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountains.

items.subject: science
items.title: San Andreas transform boundary
items.summary: The San Andreas Fault is where the Pacific plate slides northwest past the North American plate. Stress builds, then releases as earthquakes, and scientists measure it to estimate hazards.

items.subject: science
items.title: Rock cycle and Earth's history
items.summary: Rocks change between igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic over millions of years. Rock layers and fossils help scientists tell Earth's long history.

items.subject: science
items.title: Science words
items.summary: Here are some science thinking words! Scientists ask questions, make hypotheses, collect evidence, and build models.

items.subject: science
items.title: Engineering design process
items.summary: Engineers define a problem, brainstorm, build a prototype, test it, and improve it. Compare designs using clear criteria like cost, safety, and effectiveness.

items.subject: science
items.title: Cells are the building blocks
items.summary: All living things are made of cells. Some are just one cell, others have trillions. Cells have parts like a nucleus that directs the cell, and a membrane that controls what comes in and out.

items.subject: science
items.title: Body systems
items.summary: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs work in body systems such as the circulatory, respiratory, and nervous systems. They cooperate to keep you alive.

items.subject: science
items.title: Photosynthesis and respiration
items.summary: In photosynthesis, plants use light, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar and oxygen. In cellular respiration, cells use oxygen to release energy from that sugar.

items.subject: science
items.title: Atoms and molecules
items.summary: Everything is made of atoms, which join into molecules. The periodic table lists the kinds of atoms, called elements. There are only about 118, yet they make everything.

items.subject: science
items.title: Chemical reactions
items.summary: In a chemical reaction, atoms rearrange to make new substances, but none are lost. Signs include gas bubbles, color change, or heat. Rust and cooking are reactions.

items.subject: science
items.title: Chemistry words
items.summary: Here are chemistry words! In a reaction, reactants change into products.

items.subject: science
items.title: Natural resources and human impact
items.summary: People use resources like water, minerals, and fuel. Using them wisely and finding renewable options reduces harm to ecosystems and the climate.

items.subject: science
items.title: California water and drought
items.summary: Most of California's rain falls in the north, but most people live in the south. Dams, canals, and snowpack move water, and droughts push us to conserve and recycle.

items.subject: science
items.title: Fire and California ecosystems
items.summary: Many California plants, like chaparral shrubs and some pines, have adapted to fire. Some cones open only in heat. But hotter, bigger fires today challenge people and nature.

items.subject: science
items.title: Ocean and tide pool systems
items.summary: California's coast has tide pools, kelp forests, and deep canyons like Monterey Bay's. Marine protected areas help keep these ecosystems healthy.

items.subject: science
items.title: Forces and motion
items.summary: Newton's laws say things keep moving the same way unless a force acts, force makes things accelerate, and every push has an equal push back. Seat belts work because of the first law.

items.subject: science
items.title: Gravity and fields
items.summary: Gravity is a pull between any two things with mass, and it's strong when one is huge like a planet. Magnets and electric charges act through fields without touching.

items.subject: science
items.title: Waves and light
items.summary: Waves carry energy. Light is an electromagnetic wave that can reflect, bend, and be absorbed. Sound needs matter to travel, but light can cross empty space.

items.subject: science
items.title: Genes and heredity
items.summary: Genes in DNA carry instructions for traits. Offspring get genes from parents, so they share traits but are not exact copies. Mutations can change genes.

items.subject: science
items.title: Natural selection
items.summary: Individuals in a species vary, and some have traits that help them survive and have babies. Over many generations those traits become more common, and species change.

items.subject: science
items.title: Evidence for evolution
items.summary: Fossils, similar bones across animals, and DNA all show living things share ancestors. Fossils from La Brea Tar Pits record Ice Age California.

items.subject: science
items.title: The solar system and the Moon
items.summary: Gravity holds the planets in orbit around the Sun. The Moon's phases and eclipses come from how the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up, and tides come from the Moon's pull.

items.subject: science
items.title: Stars and galaxies
items.summary: The Sun is one star in the Milky Way, a galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars. The universe holds countless galaxies and began about 13.8 billion years ago.

items.subject: science
items.title: Physics and life words
items.summary: Here are some middle school science words! Force makes things accelerate, and a gene is a chunk of DNA.

items.subject: science
items.title: Earthquake engineering
items.summary: California builders use base isolators, flexible steel, and strict codes so buildings can ride out earthquakes. Early warning apps can alert you seconds before shaking arrives.
